title: Justin's Sunday (First Apology 65–67)
hookLine: read his whole description of a second-century Mass
tomorrow: what do you do with a dragon lying under your ladder?

cards: Rumors grow fastest around a closed door. Outsiders whispered about what Christians did when they met.

So a teacher named Justin did something bold: he wrote the whole gathering out, step by step, and addressed it to the emperor. Readings, preaching, prayers, bread and wine, one loud Amen, a collection. Nothing hidden.
Was that wise? Christians have answered that two ways.

teach.b: In the old Schaff translation: "And on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits."

Then the one presiding urges everyone to imitate what they heard. All stand and pray. Bread and a cup of wine mixed with water are brought, the presider gives thanks at length, and the people answer: Amen.

Justin says this food is called the Eucharist, and it isn't received as common bread. Deacons carry a share to anyone who couldn't come, and the collection goes to orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers.

teach.h: THE OPEN DOOR: NOTHING TO FEAR.
teach.b: Second, the case for the open door. Justin wanted the rumors gone. Let outsiders see it plainly, and they'll find nothing to fear.
Third, the case for the veil. Some later teachers chose differently. Cyril of Jerusalem, teaching people preparing for baptism, asked them not to repeat the mysteries to outsiders.

teach.h: THE VEIL: BETTER MET THAN TOLD.
teach.b: Not to hide anything shameful, but because some holy things are better met than described. Fourth, where Catholics stand now.
Both instincts live in the Mass.
The doors are open, and anyone may come and watch every step. Communion itself is for Catholics prepared to receive it. And the Catechism quotes Justin's description when it explains the Mass.

how: Catholics gather for Mass on Sunday; anyone may attend, Communion is received by Catholics prepared to receive it, and the Catechism quotes Justin's description when it explains the shape of the Mass.

games.q: your friend says the Mass should be explained to anyone, anytime, the way Justin did. you're asked to give the best case for the other side. what is it?
o: some holy things are better met than described.
outsiders can't be trusted to understand the truth.
secrecy makes people curious, so more of them join.
games.why: Cyril of Jerusalem asked people preparing for baptism not to repeat the mysteries to outsiders, out of reverence, not suspicion. Catholics keep both: open doors, and Communion for those prepared.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write Justin's steps down the left side: readings, preaching, prayers, bread and wine, the Amen, the gift. Down the right, write what you remember from the last Mass or gathering you went to.
Draw a line wherever the two match.

wordCard.voice: Justin's Sunday. A Christian gathering written out in full, so outsiders could see there was nothing to fear.

orig.note: Greek for thanksgiving: Justin says this is what the food is called among Christians.

carryVoice: Keep this: the same sunday, read out to an emperor, still recognizable in a parish this week. Go well.
